title: Nowhere and everywhere
hook: reading too many authors scatters you: the one who is everywhere is nowhere

segments.voice: Yesterday: hold every hour, Seneca's first letter. Your line was hold this hour. Did one hour today go where you sent it? Day four hundred thirty-three.

Fourteen browser tabs. Three half-read books by the bed. Two podcasts paused in the middle. A language app, a cooking channel, a course you paid for in January. None of it bad. All of it started. Very little finished. If that's familiar, you're in good company: Lucilius seems to have had a version of the same problem, and Seneca's second letter is his answer. We met one line of this letter back in year one, about reading slowly. Today we go underneath it, to the restlessness itself. Today: nowhere and everywhere.
screen: `FOURTEEN TABS OPEN.` → `ALL STARTED, LITTLE FINISHED.` → `NOWHERE AND EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: First, the good sign. Seneca opens kindly. He's heard that Lucilius isn't rushing from place to place, and he takes it as a sign of a settled mind. A mind in order, he says, can stop and spend time with itself. Second, the restlessness. Then the warning. Be careful, he says, that reading many authors and every kind of book doesn't make you just as restless as constant travel. In Gummere's translation, three words: Everywhere means nowhere. Third, the pictures. Seneca piles them up. A person who spends all their life traveling ends up with many acquaintances and no friends. Food that comes straight back up doesn't nourish the body. A wound doesn't heal if you keep changing the medicine. A plant that's moved again and again can't grow strong roots. Every picture says the same thing: depth needs staying. Fourth, the cure. So stay with a few, Seneca says, and let them sink in. When you feel like a change, go back to someone you've already read. And each day take away one thought to digest. That's why this day's line is go deep. Not because new things are bad: Seneca himself goes on to quote Epicurus, a philosopher from a rival school, because a good thought is good wherever it comes from. But you can't take root in fourteen places at once. The restless person isn't everywhere. They're nowhere for very long. The one who stays can finally arrive.
screen: `A SETTLED MIND CAN STAY.` · `EVERYWHERE MEANS NOWHERE.` · `THE PLANT MOVED TOO OFTEN.` · `STAY WITH A FEW; DIGEST ONE.` · then, large: `GO DEEP.`

segments.voice: Take one short thing to read: a line you love, a verse, a paragraph from a book nearby, even today's line, go deep. Read it once, at normal speed. Then close your eyes and breathe. Now read it again, slower, as if you'd never seen it. Notice one word you missed the first time. Stay with that word. Let it sink like a stone into still water, down and down, until it rests on the bottom. The bell holds the time.
Nowhere and everywhere. Seneca's second letter: the restless reader, like the restless traveler, scatters themselves; the one who stays with a few can take root. Today's word.
Your line: go deep. Read one thing twice today instead of two things once. Close one tab you'll never get to. Day four hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Readers following Seneca's advice often stay with a few trusted authors, reread rather than skim, and take away one thought each day to carry.

original.note: Latin: the one who is everywhere is nowhere, from Seneca's second letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about reading lists.
what it means: Seneca says restlessness, in books or travel, scatters a person; staying with a few is how you take root.
what a scholar hears: the early letters often end with a gift line from Epicurus, a rival school, and Seneca defends quoting him as fair borrowing.
